Extraordinary Means
ek-struh-OR-din-ehr-ee MEENZ
n. phrase (Reformed bibliology / cessationism)
From Latin extraordinarius (outside the ordinary order, exceptional) + media (means, instruments). Extraordinary means refer to divine acts and revelatory instruments outside the normal, repeatable channels of Word, sacrament, and prayer—including miracles, angelic visitation, direct prophetic utterance, and sign gifts—characteristic of the foundational and apostolic eras but not the present ordinary-means age.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Extraordinary means are the exceptional, non-repeatable instruments by which God revealed Himself and confirmed the apostolic foundation in the early church. They stand in contrast to the ordinary means (Word, sacrament, prayer), which are the permanent and sufficient channels of grace for every generation. The letter to the Hebrews draws the theological line explicitly: “God, after He spoke long ago to the fathers in the prophets—in many parts and in many ways—in these last days has spoken to us in His Son” (Heb 1:1–2). The “many parts and many ways” of the former era included dreams, theophanies, direct prophetic revelation, and miraculous signs. The Son is the culmination and conclusion of that revelatory series. Paul acknowledges that the partial gives way to the complete: “when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away” (1 Cor 13:10). The apostolic gift of prophecy, tongues, and healing signs served a foundational purpose—confirming the apostolic message and establishing the church before the canon was complete. Deuteronomy provides the test for authentic prophetic utterance: “if the thing does not happen or come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD has not spoken” (Deut 18:22). The closed Revelation closes the canon against addition: “if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues that are written in this book” (Rev 22:18). Reformed cessationism holds that the extraordinary means served their purpose in the apostolic era and have been withdrawn—not because God cannot act extraordinarily but because He has committed His people to the ordinary means as fully sufficient for all they need.

Webster 1828 Definition

The exceptional divine instruments of the apostolic foundational era—miracles, direct revelation, sign gifts—which served to confirm the gospel and establish the canon and have ceased with the close of the apostolic age, leaving the ordinary means fully sufficient.

EXTRAORDINARY MEANS, n. phrase. In Reformed and cessationist theology, the non-repeatable, exceptional divine instruments by which God revealed and confirmed the apostolic gospel—miracles, prophecy, tongues, angelic appearances, healing signs.

These means were “extraordinary” in the sense of being outside the established order: God intervened in ways not expected or normative in the ordinary church life. They authenticated the apostolic messengers and their message before the full canon was inscripturated.

The cessationist position (the Reformed and confessional default): the extraordinary means were tied to the apostolic foundational era (Eph 2:20—prophets and apostles as the foundation) and ceased when that foundation was complete. The ordinary means are now fully sufficient.

Continuationists argue the extraordinary means continue in principle, though most allow for a diminished form. The New Apostolic Reformation goes further, claiming a full restoration of apostles and prophets with genuine revelatory authority—a position the Reformed tradition identifies as an assault on the closed canon and the sufficiency of the ordinary means.

Providential extraordinary acts (remarkable answers to prayer, unusual converging circumstances, God's singular preservation of a person or people) are distinguished from charismatic sign gifts: the former are not foreclosed; the latter, as public credential-confirming miraculous gifts, belong to the apostolic era.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 1:1–2 — "God, after He spoke long ago to the fathers in the prophets — in many parts and in many ways — in these last days has spoken to us in His Son. He appointed Him heir of all things, through whom He also made the world."

1 Corinthians 13:10 — "But when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away."

Deuteronomy 18:22 — "when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the thing does not happen or come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously; you shall not be afraid of him."

Revelation 22:18 — "I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues that are written in this book."

Modern Corruption

Continuationism and the New Apostolic Reformation collapse the distinction between the foundational apostolic era and the present age, claiming all extraordinary means are ongoing and normative. This assaults the closed canon, undermines the sufficiency of Scripture, and displaces the ordinary means.

expand to see more

The New Apostolic Reformation (NAR) makes the clearest claim to restored extraordinary means: it asserts that modern apostles receive new binding revelation and modern prophets deliver new propositional words from God for the church. By Deuteronomy's standard (Deut 18:22), many such prophecies have demonstrably failed, yet the movement continues to credential its leaders by claimed extraordinary gifts rather than by the apostolic test of verified fulfillment. When extraordinary means are claimed without the apostolic foundation already laid, they displace the ordinary means and the canon alike—implying that God's people need something beyond Scripture to function. The Reformation answer is that the Son has spoken the final word (Heb 1:2); the canon is closed; and that final word is fully sufficient.

A softer continuationism holds that sign gifts continue but in a reduced or fallible form. This position—associated with Wayne Grudem's “open but cautious” framework and the Third Wave movement—attempts to maintain canonical sufficiency while allowing ongoing prophetic impressions. But by making prophecy fallible and ongoing, it creates a second track of guidance alongside Scripture that inevitably rivals it in practice. The Reformed cessationist insists the distinction must be maintained clearly: extraordinary means served the foundation; ordinary means serve the building. The foundation is laid (1 Cor 3:11; Eph 2:20); the building continues by the ordinary means alone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the biblical pattern of dramatic interventions in the foundational eras of redemptive history (Exodus, prophetic era, apostolic age), distinguished from the ordinary means and understood by Reformed cessationists as having fulfilled their foundational purpose.

expand to see more

Latin extraordinarius — outside the ordinary order, exceptional; what God does through channels not regularly appointed or expected in the church's ongoing life.

Heb 1:1–2 — the Hebrews prologue identifies the pattern: God spoke through prophets (extraordinary revelation) and now speaks in the Son (the definitive extraordinary Word now inscripturated).

Eph 2:20 — the church built on the foundation of apostles and prophets; once the foundation is laid, the extraordinary credential-signs that accompanied its laying are no longer needed.

Deut 18:22 — the prophetic test; its existence assumes that genuine extraordinary prophecy was possible—and that false claims could be identified by non-fulfillment.

Rev 22:18 — the canonical closure; any claim to add new revelation after the apostolic deposit is condemned—the clearest biblical ground for cessationism of propositional extraordinary means.

Usage

"The extraordinary means served their purpose in the apostolic era: they confirmed the gospel, authenticated the apostles, and established the canon that now makes them unnecessary."

"Cessationism is not a denial that God can act outside normal channels; it is the conviction that He has committed His people to the ordinary means as fully sufficient and that seeking extraordinary means is faithlessness toward what He has given."

"Providence still works singularly and surprisingly, but the Reformed distinction holds: providential wonders are not the same as the apostolic sign gifts, and neither restores the foundational extraordinary means that accompanied the laying of the apostolic foundation."
